paragraphs.heading: What granite is
paragraphs.text: Granite is a coarse-grained igneous rock made mostly of quartz, alkali feldspar, mica and plagioclase. It is an intrusive rock: it forms from magma that cools slowly and turns solid underground. That magma has a high content of silica and alkali metal oxides. The name comes from the Latin granum, a grain, pointing to the coarse-grained structure of this fully crystalline rock.

paragraphs.heading: Where it is found
paragraphs.text: Granite is common in Earth's continental crust, where it occurs in igneous intrusions. The smallest are dikes only centimeters across; the largest are batholiths, exposed over hundreds of square kilometers. Granitic rock is the most abundant basement rock lying under the relatively thin sedimentary cover of the continents, and much of it was intruded during the Precambrian. Batholiths are often associated with orogenic mountain ranges.

paragraphs.heading: What it looks like
paragraphs.text: Granites can be mainly white, pink or gray, depending on their minerals. Feldspar and quartz form an interlocking matrix, with darker biotite mica and amphibole scattered through the lighter minerals like pepper. Sometimes single crystals, called phenocrysts, are larger than the rest. That texture is called porphyritic, and a granitic rock that has it is a granite porphyry. Granite is nearly always massive, meaning it lacks internal structures, and it is tough.

paragraphs.heading: Drawing the line
paragraphs.text: Granite is the typical member of a larger family of granitic rocks, or granitoids, which are mostly coarse-grained quartz and feldspars mixed in varying proportions. Geologists sort them by how much quartz, alkali feldspar and plagioclase they hold relative to one another. True granite holds between 20% and 60% quartz by volume, and alkali feldspar makes up 35% to 90% of its total feldspar. Granitic rocks with less quartz are called syenites or monzonites, while those dominated by plagioclase are granodiorites or tonalites.

paragraphs.heading: Granite in numbers
paragraphs.text: Granite's average density is between 2.65 and 2.75 g/cm³, and its compressive strength usually lies above 200 MPa. Dry granite at ambient pressure melts at 1215–1260 °C. Water lowers that strongly: at a pressure of a few hundred megapascals, the melting temperature falls to 650 °C.

paragraphs.heading: In the landscape and in use
paragraphs.text: Where granite crops out, it tends to form tors, domes or bornhardts, and rounded massifs. Because it is tough and massive, granite has been a widespread construction stone throughout human history. Granite also has close relatives. Its medium-grained equivalent is microgranite, and its extrusive igneous equivalent is rhyolite.
